Occurrences.Kwic: 莫有同生同死底麼？出來與徑山拄杖子相見。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X64/X64n1260.xml). Chan Grove Collection: Dahui Zonggao asks whether anyone will live and die together with him and calls that person out to meet the staff of Jingshan.

Occurrences.Kwic: 還有同生同死底衲僧麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J32/J32nB272.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Hongzhi Jue: Hongzhi Zhengjue raises Fengxue’s paired alternatives and asks whether a patch-robed monk will live and die together with him under them.

Occurrences.Kwic: 直下與三世諸佛同生同死。與火焰同起同滅。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1997.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo: Yuanwu Keqin says that seeing through the fire sermon means directly living and dying with the buddhas of the three times and arising and ceasing with the flames.

Occurrences.Kwic: 具七事隨身。可以同生同死。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2003.xml). Blue Cliff Record: Yuanwu Keqin says the cited named speaker equipped with the seven provisions can live and die together with people, entering the same cauldron and furnace to free them from bonds.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雖然如是，同生同死，遮裏放過則不可。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J33/J33nB280.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yunwai Xingze: At a memorial address Yunwai Xingze extends sameness through birth and death, then refuses to let “living and dying together” pass as a merely verbal conclusion.

Source record (X/X82/X82n1571.xml). Complete Collection of the Five Lamps: An unnamed monk asks Fushan Dexuan what “living and dying together” is after Fushan answers a question about Buddha; Fushan answers by challenging whether the explicit unnamed questioner may be called Buddha.

Senses.Explanation: To live and die together is to share the same exposure in a Chan encounter: the exact named speaker calls for someone who will stand with him through the case rather than remain a spectator. Dahui Zonggao asks whether anyone will live and die together with him, then calls that person out to meet his staff. Hongzhi Zhengjue likewise asks for a patch-robed monk who will do so after raising Fengxue’s opposed alternatives. These are public challenges, not descriptions of two people sharing dates of birth and death. Yuanwu Keqin applies the phrase to the cited named speaker who enters the same cauldron and furnace as the person being freed, and elsewhere to going through the fire sermon with the buddhas of the three times. Yunwai Xingze uses it in a memorial address but immediately refuses to let the phrase pass without a further test. An unnamed monk asks Fushan Dexuan directly what living and dying together is; Fushan turns the question back on whether the explicit unnamed questioner may be called Buddha. The sources repeatedly mark shared exposure, accompaniment, or matched commitment under a live test. They do not make the phrase a promise of literal simultaneous death, nor do they supply one abstract theory behind every case.
